To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

acute ethanol pretreatment potentiates angiotensin-induced NaCl intake, neuropeptide Y-induced food intake, and angiotensin- and neuropeptide Y-elicited drinking, and inhibits pituitary oxytoxin secretion, and that oxytocin administration into the brain ventricles prevents ethanol-induced potentiation.
ethanol potentiately stimulates NaCl and food ingestion in rats, in a manner that is consistent with its ability to suppress pituitary oxytotocin secretion.
ethanol potentiating effects on salt and food ingestion are mediated, at least in part, by the inhibition of central oxytocinergic activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurochemical basis of ethanol's effects on ingestive behaviors.
the effects of ethanol on salt appetite, food intake, and the release of oxytocin.
the acute effects of ethanol on the ingestion of various nutrients and the mechanisms by which ethanol exerts its acute effects on ingestive behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the acute ethanol-induced potentiation on salt appetite and food intake is mediated by the inhibition of oxytocin release from the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus.
acute ethanol administration potentiates the ingestive effects of neuropeptide Y and angiotensin, but blunts oxytocin-induced ingestive behavior in adult rats.
ethanol is a potent stimulant for the ingestion of various substances, but that the mechanisms by which it does so are not fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ethanol inhibits the release of central oxytocin, which in turn disinhibits ingestive behavior.
ethanol inhibits oxytocinergic projections to the brain and, as a result, increases ingestive behavior in the rat.

the acute effects of ethanol on the ingestion of solutes are complex, and that the effects of ethanol on pituitary oxytotocin secretion and on the central oxytocinergic system may contribute to these effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oxytocin is a critical modulator of ingestive behaviors and ethanol-induced alterations in ingestive behaviors may involve oxytocin.
ethanol potentiating effects on ingestive behavior can be dissociated from the inhibitory effects on pituitary oxytoic secretion.
ethanol can modulate ingestive behaviors in rats, in particular, salt appetite.
